title: Rumours that moved armies
dek: Before a fact can travel, a story often already has. Some campaigns have been steered by what people were sure they had heard.
speakingPrompts: Retell a historical panic in two minutes, then name the missing verification step.
How is a wartime rumour different from a false memory — and how are they cousins?
What rule would you give a newsroom during the first hour of an unfolding event?

blocks.text: History is full of dispatches that were wrong on purpose, and a more interesting set that were wrong by accident and still did work. A rumour is a social memory in draft form: vivid, poorly sourced, easy to repeat. Armies have marched toward ghosts. Crowds have emptied cities. Markets have crashed on a sentence that never had an owner.

In crises, verification is expensive and delay can be fatal. That incentive structure is older than the internet. During the French Revolution, the Great Fear of 1789 spread as a chain of alarms about brigands and aristocratic plots. Some local threats were real; the nationwide pattern was a contagion of expectation. People acted on what their neighbours believed, which made the belief locally true enough to matter: they armed, they burned, they waited.

The psychology shelf of Curio is not a detour here. Source monitoring fails in groups too. A story with a face and a direction of threat outruns a cautious “we do not yet know.” Leaders know this and sometimes plant rumours. More often they are captured by them, forced to respond to a public that has already written the first paragraph.

blocks.title: A historian’s hygiene
blocks.text: When a secondary source says “news spread that…”, ask: along which roads, in whose accent, with what incentive to exaggerate? Rumour has a geography. Mapping it is often more revealing than judging it.

We still move resources toward stories that feel finished. The discipline is not cynicism. It is slowing the conversion of a vivid report into a march. Five minutes of asking “who saw it, who benefits, what would falsify it?” is an unglamorous civic skill. History’s rumours are a museum of what happens when that minute is skipped.
